claim: Nomograms are important clinical tools applied widely in both developing and aging populations.
source: Nomograms are important clinical tools applied widely in both developing and aging populations.
evidence: This is a general statement about nomograms in the abstract, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Nomograms are generally constructed as normative models identifying cases as outliers to a distribution of healthy controls.
source: They are generally constructed as normative models identifying cases as outliers to a distribution of healthy controls.
evidence: This describes the standard methodology for nomogram construction, based on established knowledge.

claim: Currently used normative models do not account for genetic heterogeneity.
source: Currently used normative models do not account for genetic heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field, supported by the authors' review of existing literature.

claim: Hippocampal volume (HV) is a key endophenotype for many brain disorders.
source: Hippocampal volume (HV) is a key endophenotype for many brain disorders.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in neuroscience and psychiatry.

claim: The study used imaging data from 35,686 healthy subjects aged 44–82 from the UK Biobank (UKB).
source: Using imaging data from 35,686 healthy subjects aged 44–82 from the UK Biobank (UKB), we built HV nomograms using Gaussian process regression (GPR)
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and describes the study's dataset.

claim: GPR extended the application age by 20 years compared to a previous method, including dementia critical age ranges.
source: which – compared to a previous method – extended the application age by 20 years, including dementia critical age ranges.
evidence: This is a finding from the study comparing GPR to the sliding window approach.

claim: Genetically adjusted nomograms were built from participants stratified into the top and bottom 30% of HV-PGS.
source: Using HV polygenic scores (HV-PGS), we built genetically adjusted nomograms from participants stratified into the top and bottom 30% of HV-PGS.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Genetic stratification shifted the nomograms in the expected directions by ~100 mm3 (2.3% of the average HV).
source: This shifted the nomograms in the expected directions by ~100 mm3 (2.3% of the average HV)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The shift in nomograms equates to 3 years of normal aging for a person aged ~65.
source: which equates to 3 years of normal aging for a person aged ~65.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data comparing the genetic effect to aging effects.

claim: 818 subjects from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database were used to investigate clinical impact.
source: Clinical impact of genetically adjusted nomograms was investigated by comparing 818 subjects from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database diagnosed as either cognitively normal (CN), having mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients.
evidence: This describes the validation dataset used in the study.

claim: No significant change in the survival analysis was found for MCI-to-AD conversion.
source: While no significant change in the survival analysis was found for MCI-to-AD conversion
evidence: This is a negative finding from the longitudinal analysis.

claim: An average of 68% relative decrease was found in intra-diagnostic-group variance with genetic adjustment.
source: an average of 68% relative decrease was found in intra-diagnostic-group variance, highlighting the importance of genetic adjustment in untangling phenotypic heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis of diagnostic groups.

claim: Normative modelling is an emerging method in neuroscience, aiming to identify cases as outliers to a distribution of healthy controls.
source: Normative modelling is an emerging method in neuroscience, aiming to identify cases as outliers to a distribution of healthy controls and was shown to have potential to improve early diagnosis, progression models, and risk assessment (Marquand et al., 2016; Pinaya et al., 2020; Wolfers et al., 2020; Ziegler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in the field.

claim: Normative models work well even when cases are not clustered or overlap with controls.
source: Where conventional case-control studies generally require both cases and controls to be well clustered, normative models work well even when cases are not clustered or overlap with controls.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of normative models, based on established knowledge.

claim: Nomograms have been used as growth charts of brain volumes across age in both developing and aging populations.
source: Nomograms are a common implementation of normative models and have been used as growth charts of brain volumes across age in both developing and aging populations (Castellanos et al., 2002; Scahill et al., 2003; Peterson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Whole brain volume is 90 ± 4.8% heritable.
source: Heritability studies have found that whole brain volume is 90 ± 4.8 heritable (Lukies et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a heritability study.

claim: Hippocampal volume (HV) is 75 ± 5% heritable.
source: hippocampal volume (HV) is 75 ± 5 (Kremen et al., 2010; Thompson et al., 2020; Hibar et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to heritability studies.

claim: Other cortical brain areas have heritability between 34% and 80%.
source: and other cortical brain areas between 34% and 80% (Rentería et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to heritability studies.

claim: Genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have identified genome-wide significant variants that explain 13 ± 1.5% of the variation in HV.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have identified genome-wide significant variants that explain 13 ± 1.5 of the variation in HV (Hibar et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a GWAS study.

claim: GWASs have identified variants that explain 34 ± 3% of variation in total cortical surface area.
source: 34 ± 3 in total cortical surface area, and 26±2% in average cortical thickness (Grasby et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a GWAS study.

claim: GWASs have identified variants that explain 26±2% of variation in average cortical thickness.
source: 34 ± 3 in total cortical surface area, and 26±2% in average cortical thickness (Grasby et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a GWAS study.

claim: The gap between estimates from GWAS hits and formal heritability estimates is termed the 'missing heritability'.
source: The gap between estimates from GWAS hits and formal heritability estimates (termed the 'missing heritability') (Manolio et al., 2009)
evidence: This is a well-established concept in genetics, supported by a citation.

claim: Missing heritability may be captured through polygenic scores (PGSs).
source: implies that less significant variants also have an influence and that it may be captured through polygenic scores (PGSs) (Foo et al., 2021; Axelrud et al., 2018; Escott-Price et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on polygenic scores.

claim: The hippocampus is integral to memory processes.
source: Damage to the hippocampus which is integral to memory processes (Bird and Burgess, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to neuroscience literature.

claim: Damage to the hippocampus has been associated with major depressive disorder.
source: has been associated with major depressive disorder (Bremner et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to clinical literature.

claim: Damage to the hippocampus has been associated with schizophrenia.
source: schizophrenia (Nelson et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to clinical literature.

claim: Damage to the hippocampus has been associated with epilepsy.
source: epilepsy (Whelan et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to clinical literature.

claim: Damage to the hippocampus has been associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: and Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Pini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to clinical literature.

claim: 7% of people over 60 are diagnosed with dementia.
source: AD is a global health burden: 7% of people over 60 are diagnosed with dementia (van der Flier and Scheltens, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to epidemiological literature.

claim: AD accounts for 70% of dementia cases.
source: of which AD accounts for 70% (Rabinovici, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to clinical literature.

claim: The pathophysiological processes underlying AD, namely amyloid and tau pathology accumulation, are thought to precede brain atrophy.
source: The pathophysiological processes underlying AD, namely amyloid and tau pathology accumulation, are thought to precede brain atrophy, which typically starts in the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe and then spreads throughout the neocortex (Rabinovici, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to AD research literature.

claim: Brain atrophy in AD typically starts in the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe and then spreads throughout the neocortex.
source: which typically starts in the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe and then spreads throughout the neocortex (Rabinovici, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to AD research literature.

claim: A recent study by Nobis et al., 2019, produced HV nomograms from UK biobank for use in clinical settings.
source: for example, a recent study by Nobis et al., 2019, produced HV nomograms from UK biobank (UKB) for use in clinical settings.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Two recent studies examined the impact of the AD-associated APOE gene, showing that APOE4/4 carriers had significantly lower HV trajectories.
source: For instance, two recent studies examined the impact of the AD-associated APOE gene (Ching et al., 2020; Veldsman et al., 2021), showing that APOE4/4 carriers had significantly lower HV trajectories.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: APOE4/4 carriers have a 10-fold risk of developing AD.
source: This effect is likely driven by AD-related disease processes since APOE4/4 carriers have a 10-fold risk of developing AD (Kim et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic epidemiology studies.

claim: In the UKB sample, 453 subjects were excluded for various conditions, 3497 for genetic ancestry, and 28 subjects were outliers, leaving a total of 35,686 subjects.
source: In the UKB sample, 453 subjects were excluded for various conditions, 3497 for genetic ancestry, and 28 subjects were outliers: leaving a total of 35,686 subjects.
evidence: This describes the data processing steps and final sample size.

claim: In the ADNI application dataset, 26 subjects were excluded for genetic ancestry, and 314 based on HV quality scores, leaving 818 subjects.
source: In the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) application dataset, 26 subjects were excluded for genetic ancestry, and 314 based on HV quality scores: leaving 818 subjects.
evidence: This describes the data processing steps and final sample size for the validation dataset.

claim: Nomograms of healthy subjects generated using the sliding window approach (SWA) and GPR method displayed similar trends.
source: Nomograms of healthy subjects generated using the sliding window approach (SWA) and GPR method displayed similar trends (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the two methods, supported by data and figures.

claim: GPR nomograms spanned the entire training dataset age range (45–82 years) compared to the SWA (52–72 years).
source: However, GPR nomograms spanned the entire training dataset age range (45–82 years) compared to the SWA (52–72 years).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the two methods.

claim: The SWA is a non-model-based approach that requires smoothing to avoid edge effects.
source: This is primarily because the SWA is a non-model-based approach that requires smoothing to avoid edge effects
evidence: This explains the methodological difference between the approaches.

claim: A Gaussian smoothing window of width 20 was used for the SWA.
source: and a Gaussian smoothing window of width 20 was used (Nobis et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a specific methodological parameter, supported by citation.

claim: The GPR extension allowed 86% of all diagnostic groups from the ADNI to be evaluated vs. 56% in the SWA nomograms.
source: This extension allowed 86% of all diagnostic groups from the ADNI to be evaluated vs. 56% in the SWA nomograms (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding showing the practical benefit of GPR, supported by data and figures.

claim: The average 50th percentile in male nomograms (4162 ± 222 mm3) was higher than the female nomograms (3883 ± 170 mm3).
source: Overall, the average 50th percentile in male nomograms (4162 ± 222) was higher than the female nomograms (3883 ± 170)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the nomogram analysis.

claim: Within each sex, right HV was larger than left HV.
source: and within each sex, right HV was larger than left HV (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, supported by figures.

claim: Along the 50th percentile, male HV declined faster (−20.3mm3/year) than female HV (−14.6mm3/year).
source: We also observed that along the 50th percentile, male HV declined faster (−20.3mm3/year) than female HV (−14.6mm3/year).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the longitudinal analysis of nomograms.

claim: In GPR nomograms, HV peaks in women at age 53.5 years with a less pronounced peak in males at 50 years.
source: Additionally, in GPR nomograms, HV peaks in women at age 53.5 years with a less pronounced peak in males at 50 years (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the nomogram analysis, supported by figures.

claim: Training the GPR model with 16,000 samples took ~1 hr on a consumer grade machine (2.3 GHz 8-Core Intel Core i9).
source: Training the GPR model with 16,000 samples took ~1 hr on a consumer grade machine (2.3 GHz 8-Core Intel Core i9).
evidence: This is a practical finding about computational efficiency.

claim: The calculated PGS showed a strong correlation with HV in the UKB data.
source: The calculated PGS, based on an earlier GWAS for average bilateral HV (Hibar et al., 2017), as expected, showed a strong correlation with HV in the UKB data.
evidence: This is a finding from the PGS analysis, with citation to the GWAS used.

claim: The PGSs showed a significant positive correlation with HV across all p-value thresholds and training sample subsets (p<2.7E-24).
source: Overall, the PGSs showed a significant positive correlation with HV across all p-value thresholds and training sample subsets (p<2.7E-24; Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the PGS analysis.

claim: PGSs explained more variance in males vs. females.
source: PGSs explained more variance in males vs. females.
evidence: This is a finding from the variance analysis.

claim: PGSs did not show detectable differences in left vs. right HV.
source: Furthermore, PGSs did not show detectable differences in left vs. right HV
evidence: This is a negative finding from the analysis.

claim: PGSs explained the most variance in mean bilateral HV.
source: and explained the most variance in mean bilateral HV (Table 1, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the variance analysis.

claim: The explained variance (R2) by the PGS across p-value threshold showed one peak at the 1E-7 threshold and a higher peak at the 0.75 threshold.
source: In all tested settings, the explained variance (R2) by the PGS across p-value threshold was similar: with one peak at the 1E-7 threshold (capturing few but very significant SNPs), a higher peak at the 0.75 threshold (capturing many SNPs with mostly small effect sizes) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the PGS analysis, supported by figures.

claim: The top and bottom 20% of PGS scores accounted for 41% of the variance in HV.
source: When investigating mean HV across percentile of PGS at the 0.75 threshold (highest R2), the top and bottom 20% of scores accounted for 41% of the variance in HV (Figure 3)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the variance analysis.

claim: The high PGS nomograms were shifted upwards while the low-PGS nomograms were shifted downwards.
source: Genetics had a clear effect on the nomograms: the high PGS nomograms were shifted upwards while the low-PGS nomograms were shifted downwards
evidence: This is a finding from the genetically adjusted nomogram analysis.

claim: Both high and low PGS nomograms were shifted by around 1.2% of the average HV (50 mm3).
source: an effect which could be observed at both the model and data level (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 3), both by around 1.2% of the average HV (50 mm3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis, supported by figures.

claim: The difference between high and low PGS nomograms was ~2.3% of the average HV (100 mm3).
source: Thus, the difference between high and low PGS nomograms was ~2.3% of the average HV (100 mm3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis.

claim: An ANOVA test of the percentiles produced with the adjusted vs. unadjusted nomograms revealed that the groups were significantly different to each other (F>19; p<8.04E-6).
source: An ANOVA test of the percentiles produced with the adjusted vs. unadjusted nomograms revealed that the groups were significantly different to each other (F>19; p<8.04E-6; Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the comparison of nomograms.

claim: The HV peak previously observed at 50 years in males was less pronounced in the high PGS nomogram and more so in the low PGS nomogram.
source: The HV peak previously observed at 50 years in males was less pronounced in the high PGS nomogram and more so in the low PGS nomogram (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the genetically adjusted nomogram analysis, supported by figures.

claim: Adjusting nomograms using ICV and AD PGSs, instead of HV PGS, did not result in nomograms that were meaningfully different from the non-adjusted nomograms.
source: Adjusting nomograms using ICV and AD PGSs, instead of HV PGS, did not result in nomograms that were meaningfully different from the non-adjusted nomograms (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the specificity analysis, supported by figures.

claim: In ADNI, cognitively normal (CN) participants (n=225) had a median bilateral HV percentile of 61% (±25% SD).
source: Using the non-adjusted nomogram, cognitively normal (CN) participants (n=225) had a median bilateral HV percentile of 61% (±25% SD)
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the ADNI validation dataset.

claim: In ADNI, mild cognitive impairment (MCI) participants (n=391) had a median bilateral HV percentile of 25% (±26% SD).
source: mild cognitive impairment (MCI) participants (n=391) had 25% (±26% SD)
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the ADNI validation dataset.

claim: In ADNI, AD participants (n=121) had a median bilateral HV percentile of 1% (±9% SD).
source: and AD participants (n=121) had 1% (±9% SD) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the ADNI validation dataset.

claim: High PGS CN samples had median percentiles of 65% (±27% SD) and low PGS had 54% (±26% SD) when compared against unadjusted nomograms.
source: Bisecting the samples by PGS showed that high PGS CN samples had median percentiles of 65% (±27% SD) and low PGS had 54% (±26% SD).
evidence: This is a finding from the stratified analysis.

claim: When comparing against genetically adjusted nomograms, high PGS CN samples had 60% (±26% SD) and low PGS had 59% (±26% SD).
source: When comparing the same samples against the genetically adjusted nomograms instead, high PGS CN samples had 60% (±26% SD) and low PGS had 59% (±26% SD).
evidence: This is a finding from the genetically adjusted analysis.

claim: Genetic adjustment reduced the gap between high and low PGS CN participants by 9% (from 10% to 1%, a 90% relative reduction).
source: Thus, reducing the gap between high and low PGS CN participants by 9% (from 10% to 1%, a 90% relative reduction).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding showing the effect of genetic adjustment.

claim: Genetic adjustment showed a reduction in MCI participants by 10% (60% relative reduction).
source: Similar analysis showed a reduction in MCI participants by 10% (60% relative reduction)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding showing the effect of genetic adjustment.

claim: Genetic adjustment showed a reduction in AD participants by 0.5% (56% relative reduction).
source: and 0.5% (56% relative reduction) in AD participants.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding showing the effect of genetic adjustment.

claim: With the non-adjusted nomogram, progressing MCI participants had a mean HV percentile of 11% and stable participants had 29%.
source: With the non-adjusted nomogram, progressing MCI participants had a mean HV percentile of 11% and stable participants had 29% (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal analysis.

claim: Using the genetically adjusted nomograms, progressing MCI participants had 10% and stable participants had 28%.
source: Using the genetically adjusted nomograms, they had 10% and 28%, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal analysis with adjusted nomograms.

claim: Cox proportional hazards models of percentiles obtained using both nomograms revealed little difference between the two in terms of clinical conversion.
source: Cox proportional hazards models of percentiles obtained using both nomograms revealed little difference between the two in terms of clinical conversion
evidence: This is a finding from the survival analysis.

claim: Both Cox models resulted in a hazard ratio of 0.97 for percentile in nomogram (beta of –0.03 at p-value<4.87E-08).
source: both models resulted in a hazard ratio of 0.97 for percentile in nomogram (beta of –0.03 at p-value<4.87E-08)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the survival analysis.

claim: Participants within lower HV percentiles were more likely to convert earlier.
source: confirming that participants within lower HV percentiles where more likely to convert earlier.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the survival analysis results.

claim: The PGS for HV was significantly positively correlated with estimated HV from MRI.
source: Indeed, the PGS for HV was significantly positively correlated with estimated HV from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis.

claim: The magnitude of the nomogram shift corresponds to ~3 years' worth of HV loss during normal aging for a 65-year-old.
source: Importantly, this magnitude corresponds to ~3 years' worth of HV loss during normal aging for a 65-year-old.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data comparing genetic effects to aging effects.

claim: The APOE genotype is associated with present or future AD status rather than having a direct influence on HV in healthy populations.
source: This is an important difference: the APOE genotype is associated with present or future AD status rather than having a direct influence on HV in healthy populations.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the literature and the study's findings.

claim: GWASs of the hippocampus that exclude dementia patients find little influence of AD-associated SNPs.
source: Indeed, GWASs of the hippocampus that exclude dementia patients find little influence of AD-associated SNPs (Hibar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a GWAS study.

claim: Accounting for the genetics of healthy variation in HV should enable earlier detection of AD-related HV decline in aging individuals.
source: Therefore, in theory, accounting for the genetics of healthy variation in HV should enable earlier detection of AD-related HV decline aging individuals.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the study's findings.

claim: Stratifying by APOE-e4 status when creating HV nomograms will theoretically decrease the sensitivity to HV decline.
source: Conversely, stratifying by APOE-e4 status when creating HV nomograms charts the different HV trajectories among APOE genotypes, however, at the same time masks the pathological decline and thus will theoretically decrease the sensitivity to HV decline.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the study's reasoning.

claim: Subjects with extreme PGS account for significant amounts of the variance as indicated by the S-shape in the quantile plots.
source: Subjects with extreme PGS account for significant amounts of the variance as indicated by the S-shape in the quantile plots (e.g., Figure 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis, supported by figures.

claim: Similar S-shaped patterns in PGS-trait combinations have been observed in other studies.
source: This has been observed in other PGS-trait combinations (Axelrud et al., 2018; Escott-Price et al., 2015; Ranlund et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: The two peaks in R2 values reflect oligogenic effects (few SNPs with high effect size) and polygenic effects (combined effect of all common genetic variants).
source: This reflects two types of genetic effects: the first is that few SNPs account for a substantial portion of the total variance in HV because of their high effect size (oligogenic effect) and the second is the combined effect of all common genetic variants on HV (polygenic effect).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the R2 pattern observed in the data.

claim: This type of genetic effect has been reported in other studies of dementia.
source: This type of effect has been reported in other studies of dementia (Bis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to another study.

claim: Using a model-based method allows generation of accurate nomograms across the entire age range of the dataset.
source: In addition to demonstrating the clear effect of genetics on normative models, we have shown GPR to be effective for estimating nomograms. Using a model-based method allows us to generate accurate nomograms across the entire age range of the dataset.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the methodological advantage of GPR.

claim: The GPR model can potentially be extended a few years beyond the training data limits.
source: In fact, our GPR model can potentially be extended a few years beyond those limits (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding about the extrapolation capability of GPR, supported by a figure.

claim: The SWA nomograms age range is reduced by 20 years compared to the range of the training because of the required smoothing.
source: In comparison, the SWA nomograms age range is reduced by 20 years compared to the range of the training because of the required smoothing.
evidence: This is a finding comparing the two methods.

claim: The study extended the age range forwards by 10 years, bringing it out to 82 years of age.
source: Thus, compared to the SWA, we extended the age range forwards by 10 years, bringing it out to 82 years of age
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the age range extension.

claim: Most AD patients display symptoms at around age 65–75.
source: which is relevant for AD where most patients display symptoms at around age 65–75 (Rabinovici, 2019; Mendez, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: The peak noted in the male nomogram is likely due to under-sampling in the younger participants.
source: For example, we suspect that the peak noted in the male nomogram is likely due to under-sampling in the younger participants.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential artifact in the data.

claim: With the SWA, using around 17% (3000 samples) of training samples generated nomograms that were on average only 0.4% of average HV (19 mm3) different to those generated by the full training set.
source: We found that building nomograms is data efficient: with the SWA, using around 17% (3000 samples) of training samples generated nomograms that were on average only 0.4% of average HV (19 mm3) different to those generated by the full training set.
evidence: This is a finding about data efficiency from the analysis.

claim: GPR nomograms achieved the same level of accuracy with only 5% (900 samples) of the dataset.
source: GPR nomograms achieved the same level of accuracy with only 5% (900 samples) of the dataset (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding about data efficiency, supported by a figure.

claim: Using PGS improves the normative modelling in an independent dataset.
source: Using PGS improves the normative modelling in an independent dataset.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the validation analysis.

claim: In ADNI genetic adjustment reduced the percentile gap between similarly diagnosed subjects with genetically predicted high and low HV.
source: In ADNI genetic adjustment reduced the percentile gap between similarly diagnosed subjects with genetically predicted high and low HV.
evidence: This is a finding from the ADNI validation analysis.

claim: The impact of the PGS adjusted model on CN samples was greater than on MCI or AD samples.
source: The impact of the PGS adjusted model on CN samples was greater than on MCI or AD samples.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis across diagnostic groups.

claim: Genetic adjustment centred the CN samples closer to the 50th percentile.
source: Genetic adjustment centred the CN samples closer to the 50th percentile.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of CN samples.

claim: The pathological effect of AD on HV (~804 mm3 or 6.4% volume loss) far exceeds the shift in nomograms achieved with genetic adjustment (~100 mm3 or 0.8% of mean HV).
source: As the effect of building separate nomograms was to mitigate the impact of genetic variability on HV it was not surprising that this effect did not carry over to MCI and AD subjects, likely because the pathological effect of AD on HV (~804 mm3 or 6.4% volume loss) far exceeds the shift in nomograms achieved with genetic adjustment (~100 mm3 or 0.8% of mean HV).
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the magnitude of genetic and pathological effects.

claim: Other studies have found that annual HV loss in CN subjects was between 0.38% and 1.73%.
source: Other studies have found that annual HV loss in CN subjects was between 0.38% and 1.73% (Scahill et al., 2003; Leong et al., 2017; Jack et al., 2000; Mori et al., 2002; Risacher et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Genetically adjusted nomograms did not provide additional insight into distinguishing MCI subjects that remained stable or converted to AD.
source: However, despite this sizable effect, genetically adjusted nomograms did not provide additional insight into distinguishing MCI subjects that remained stable or converted to AD.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the longitudinal analysis.

claim: The added precision from genetic adjustment may prove more useful in early detection of deviation among CN subjects.
source: Nonetheless, the added precision may prove more useful in early detection of deviation among CN subjects, for instance in detecting subtle HV loss in individuals with presymptomatic neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential future applications.

source: Integrating the PGSs into the GP models would remove the need for stratification and allow for more adjustment precision
evidence: This is a suggestion for future methodological improvement.

source: however, PGSs are prone to 'site' effects depending on the method and quality of genotyping and imputation.
evidence: This is a known limitation of PGS methods, based on established knowledge.

claim: FreeSurfer is known to consistently overestimate HV.

source: Therefore, other brain regions with higher SNP heritability like the cerebellum or whole brain volume (Zhao et al., 2019) may show more sensitivity on nomograms.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to a methodological study.
